summary: Marcus is confronted by a teacher, Mr. Ryan's counterpart unnamed in this excerpt, after a video feed showed him protesting a social studies lesson he saw as propaganda claiming the Constitution did not matter. The teacher invokes zero-tolerance and demands an apology; Marcus refuses, recites the Declaration of Independence's passage on governments deriving power from the consent of the governed, and is suspended for two weeks. He goes home, drops the letter on the kitchen table, and turns on the TV, where the news about American soldiers dying abroad and general fear shape his parents' view of the world.
one_line: Marcus is suspended for two weeks after defending the Constitution against a teacher's lesson, then sees the fearful news his parents follow at home.
key_facts: The teacher watched Marcus through the video feed from the social studies classroom.
Marcus said the lesson 'wasn't teaching, it was propaganda' and claimed the teacher 'told us that the Constitution didn't matter!'
The teacher said the lesson 'wasn't religious doctrine' and accused Marcus of attacking her 'like some kind of fundamentalist'.
The teacher said 'everything changed when the bridge was bombed' and mentioned Marcus's friend Darryl.
Marcus told the teacher 'We used to be a free country. Now we're not.'
The teacher warned Marcus about 'zero-tolerance' and said he could expel him for 'threatening behavior'.
The teacher demanded an apology, which Marcus refused, deciding he 'would rather get kicked out than apologize'.
Marcus recited the Declaration of Independence passage beginning 'Governments are instituted among men, deriving their just powers from the consent of the governed'.
The teacher replied 'Remembering things isn't the same as understanding them, sonny.'
Marcus was suspended for two weeks, and the teacher said he would email Marcus's parents.
The teacher said Marcus would be arrested for trespassing if still on school property in thirty minutes.
Marcus threw the suspension letter on the kitchen table when he got home.
Marcus's parents got their ideas about the world from the TV, radio and newspapers.
The news Marcus saw said American soldiers were dying all over the world, including National guardsmen.
